# Results — Study 498 (Dual Thrust)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a break of
the opening-range trigger catches the day's trend: buy when the close clears
`open + k1·Range`** — encoded as a mechanical rule. The Range is the trailing-`N` span
`max(HH−LC, HC−LL)` computed on bars strictly before today (known at the open, no look-ahead);
a long fires on the first close above the buy line, entered at the **next close** (one
documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once
cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Parameters | Chalek lookback **N = 5**, trigger coefficients **k1 = k2 = 0.5** |
| Entries | **1 251** mechanical upper-trigger breakouts pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | Range from the **prior N bars** (known at the open); enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per trade |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — breakout vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch breakout-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = breakout − random.

| horizon | n | breakout | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (brk−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 1250 | +2.6 bps | 54% | +0.36 | +35.8 bps | **−33.1 bps** | +0.6 bps | **−3.39** | 0.001 |
| 10-day | 1249 | +41.5 bps | 59% | +3.96 | +76.2 bps | **−34.6 bps** | +39.5 bps | **−2.63** | 0.009 |
| 20-day | 1247 | +84.0 bps | 62% | +4.84 | +139.2 bps | **−55.2 bps** | +82.0 bps | **−2.80** | 0.005 |
| 60-day | 1243 | +219.4 bps | 66% | +5.42 | +366.5 bps | **−147.1 bps** | +217.4 bps | **−4.48** | 0.000 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks fine (**+4.84** at 20 days, **+5.42**
at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit the
drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the breakout is **worse at every single
horizon**, and the breakout-minus-random difference is **significantly negative** (Welch *t* =
−3.39 / −2.63 / −2.80 / −4.48, all *p* ≤ 0.01). This is not "no edge" — it is a **negative**
edge: the breakout *systematically buys after price has already run up*, paying a worse entry
than a coin flip. The Dual-Thrust trigger anti-forecasts.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the breakout loses to random everywhere

| ticker | entries | breakout | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (brk−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 236 | +83.0 bps | +2.25 | +107.5 bps | **−24.5 bps** |
| QQQ | 270 | +91.9 bps | +2.37 | +160.4 bps | **−68.5 bps** |
| IWM | 266 | +75.8 bps | +1.90 | +160.3 bps | **−84.5 bps** |
| DIA | 264 | +71.3 bps | +2.40 | +121.2 bps | **−49.9 bps** |
| GLD | 215 | +101.0 bps | +2.50 | +143.1 bps | **−42.1 bps** |

The breakout underperforms a dart-throwing entry in **all 5 of 5** names. No coherent
cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled (and, here, mistimed) drift.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the Range, nothing changes

The decisive "does the geometry matter?" test: keep the Range **marginal** (the same set of
band-widths) and the `k` coefficients, but permute **which day** each Range belongs to, so the
buy line at any date is built from a Range that no longer matches that date's trailing window.
If price genuinely respected *this specific opening-range geometry*, the scramble would collapse
the result.

| test | observed breakout 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-Range bands | +83.0 bps | **0.942** | 500 |

**94% of scrambled-Range bands match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.942). The Dual-Thrust
geometry carries no information — a random band width does just as well. "The opening-range
breakout forecasts" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real continuation

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* breakout-continuation (knob `edge`), the same upper-
trigger rule behaves exactly as it must vs the random baseline — so the negative real-tape
result is a genuine "nothing there (worse than nothing)", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | breakout | win% | random | Δ vs random | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no continuation) | 438 | +73.9 bps | 54% | +65.9 bps | **+8.0 bps** | +0.25 | 0.802 |
| **2.00** (real planted continuation) | 279 | +360.6 bps | 64% | +118.3 bps | **+242.3 bps** | **+3.25** | 0.001 |

With no planted continuation the breakout does **not** beat random (Δ = +8 bps, Welch *t* =
+0.25 — no false positive); a real planted continuation lights up at Welch *t* = +3.25
(Δ = +242 bps). The detector is live — it banks a true breakout edge when one exists.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The Dual-Thrust breakout does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  — it is **significantly worse** at every horizon (breakout − random = −33 / −35 / −55 / −147
  bps at 5/10/20/60 days; Welch *t* = −3.39 / −2.63 / −2.80 / −4.48, all *p* ≤ 0.01). The
  fine-looking one-sample *t*'s (20-day +4.84, 60-day +5.42) are pure beta — the upward drift of
  long equity indices, *mistimed*: the rule chases price after it has already moved.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift is removed — in fact the
  rule earns *less* than the drift it inherits, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift
  is captured more cheaply and more fully by holding the index; the breakout rule trades on
  triggers and pays costs on each, dominating nothing.
- **"Does the range breakout forecast?" — BUSTED.** The scrambled-Range placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.942): a random band width does as well as the real Dual-Thrust Range,
  so the specific opening-range geometry carries no forecasting information. Dual Thrust is an
  intraday-trend *description*, not a daily forecasting edge.
